Pulmonary Disorders

Pneumothorax

Pneumothorax is air in the pleural space. The ED task is not just naming it on x-ray; it is deciding whether the patient is unstable, whether underlying lung disease lowers reserve, and whether air must be removed immediately.

Board trap: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. Do not wait for imaging when obstructive shock and respiratory distress point to pleural pressure physiology.

PNEUMOTHORAX

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Spontaneous pneumothorax may be primary, occurring without known lung disease, or secondary, occurring with a diseased lung. Primary cases are classically seen in young, tall, thin male smokers, but any patient can present with sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. Secondary pneumothorax is more dangerous because COPD, cystic fibrosis, necrotizing infection, interstitial lung disease, malignancy, connective tissue disease, or HIV-related lung disease leaves less physiologic reserve.

Traumatic and iatrogenic pneumothoraces follow the same physiology but different workflows. This chapter focuses on ED recognition and management of spontaneous and procedure-related pneumothorax while preserving the Tintinalli treatment structure.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

The visceral and parietal pleura normally maintain negative intrapleural pressure that keeps the lung expanded. When air enters the pleural space, the pressure gradient is lost and the ipsilateral lung recoils. A small pneumothorax may cause only pain, but a large pneumothorax can reduce vital capacity and cause hypoxemia.

Tension physiology occurs when air enters during inspiration and cannot escape during expiration. Rising intrathoracic pressure collapses the lung, shifts mediastinal structures, impairs venous return, and can progress to cardiovascular collapse. Rosen illustrates this one-way valve mechanism explicitly; Tintinalli anchors it to immediate ED decompression.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Symptoms usually begin suddenly with ipsilateral pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. The pain may be sharp and can radiate to the shoulder or back. Symptoms can improve over hours even while the pneumothorax persists, so improvement alone should not end the evaluation. Physical exam is often insensitive; unilateral decreased breath sounds, hyperresonance, tachypnea, or tachycardia may be present, but small pneumothoraces can have normal findings.

In tension pneumothorax, look for severe dyspnea, hypoxemia, hypotension, distended neck veins, and obstructive shock. Tracheal deviation is late and absence of deviation does not exclude tension. In secondary pneumothorax, even a small air collection can cause substantial symptoms because baseline pulmonary reserve is limited.

DIAGNOSIS

Diagnosis combines bedside stability assessment with imaging when the patient can safely wait. A stable patient can undergo chest radiography or point-of-care ultrasound; an unstable patient with suspected tension pneumothorax should be decompressed immediately. Differential considerations include bullae, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, ACS, pericardial disease, pleural effusion, and musculoskeletal pain.

IMAGING

Chest Radiograph

An upright PA chest radiograph usually shows a visceral pleural line separated from the chest wall with no peripheral lung markings. A supine film can hide the pleural line and instead show a deep sulcus sign. Expiratory films add little and should not delay care. Size estimates vary by system; Rosen adds the Rhea method, while Tintinalli emphasizes that clinical stability and comorbidity drive decisions more than a single measurement.

US

Point-of-care ultrasound is useful at the bedside, especially when the patient is supine or radiography is delayed. Normal sliding and B-lines argue strongly against pneumothorax at the scanned site. Pneumothorax is suggested by absent lung sliding, absent B-lines, a barcode/stratosphere M-mode pattern, and a lung point. US is regional: scan the most anterior chest in supine patients and interpret findings with the clinical picture.

Chest CT

Chest CT is most sensitive for occult pneumothorax and for distinguishing pneumothorax from large bullae or other lung disease. It is useful in stable patients with unclear x-ray findings, suspected associated disease, or secondary pneumothorax where treatment planning depends on anatomy. It is not the first step for an unstable patient with suspected tension physiology.

TREATMENT

Treatment has two goals: remove pleural air when needed and reduce recurrence risk. Stable patients with a small primary pneumothorax may be observed with oxygen and serial exams, while large, symptomatic, secondary, ventilated, traumatic, or persistent air leak cases usually need active drainage. Do not let a treatment table replace treatment reasoning: stability, symptoms, size, lung reserve, and follow-up decide the pathway.

NEEDLE DECOMPRESSION

Needle decompression is a temporizing emergency procedure for suspected tension pneumothorax. Insert a large-bore catheter over the superior rib margin to avoid the neurovascular bundle, commonly at the second intercostal space midclavicular line or the fourth/fifth intercostal space anterior to midaxillary line. Adult chest wall thickness often requires a catheter at least 5 cm long. Successful decompression buys time; tube thoracostomy or definitive pleural drainage still follows.

Tintinalli source

Figure 68-4

Needle placement for decompression.

NEEDLE OR CATHETER ASPIRATION

Needle or catheter aspiration is an option for selected stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax patients, especially first episodes without severe symptoms. Large aspirated volumes or rapid recurrence suggests an ongoing leak and failure of simple aspiration. Follow-up imaging and reassessment are mandatory.

Small-Size Catheters

Small-bore catheters can drain air effectively with less discomfort than large tubes in selected patients. They are reasonable for many spontaneous pneumothoraces but are less appropriate when blood, pus, mechanical ventilation, or major trauma is part of the problem.

Pigtail Catheters Using Seldinger Technique

Pigtail catheters use wire-guided Seldinger technique and can be connected to a water seal, Heimlich valve, or suction depending on clinical need. Placement requires the same respect for sterile technique, pleural anatomy, and postprocedure confirmation as larger tubes.

Tintinalli source

Table 68-3

Aspiration and thoracostomy devices.

Tube Thoracostomy

Tube thoracostomy is used for large or symptomatic pneumothorax, secondary pneumothorax with poor reserve, traumatic pneumothorax, pneumothorax on positive-pressure ventilation, failed aspiration, hemopneumothorax, or persistent air leak. The triangle of safety helps avoid neurovascular and abdominal injury while placing the tube in a controlled lateral chest location.

Tintinalli source

Figure 68-5

Triangle of safety for chest tube placement.

TREATMENT COMPLICATIONS

Complications include tube malposition, failure to drain, persistent air leak, reexpansion pulmonary edema, bleeding from intercostal vessels, lung parenchymal injury, infection, empyema, pain, and recurrent pneumothorax. A postprocedure chest radiograph or other confirmation is part of the procedure, not an optional extra.

SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS

IATROGENIC PNEUMOTHORAX

Iatrogenic pneumothorax follows thoracentesis, lung biopsy, central venous access, barotrauma, and other procedures. Ultrasound guidance reduces thoracentesis risk, but delayed symptoms still occur. Small asymptomatic iatrogenic pneumothoraces may be observed when the patient is stable and not requiring positive-pressure ventilation; symptomatic, enlarging, or ventilated patients need drainage.

AIR TRANSPORT WITH PNEUMOTHORAX

Air trapped in the pleural space can expand as cabin pressure decreases. Patients should avoid commercial air travel until the pneumothorax has completely resolved, commonly for 7 to 14 days after radiographic resolution depending on circumstance and policy. High-altitude transport with an untreated pneumothorax can convert a stable problem into tension physiology.

DIVING

Diving creates major pressure shifts and recurrence risk. A history of spontaneous pneumothorax is generally a contraindication to scuba diving unless definitive surgical prevention has been performed and normal pulmonary function is documented by an appropriate specialist.

DISPOSITION

Disposition depends on pneumothorax type and size, symptoms, comorbidity, stability after treatment, and follow-up reliability. Stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax patients may be discharged after successful observation or aspiration if symptoms improve, imaging is stable, and recheck care is arranged. Secondary pneumothorax, persistent symptoms, recurrent air, unreliable follow-up, need for suction, or any instability favors admission. Discharge instructions must include return precautions for worsening dyspnea, pain, syncope, fever, or device malfunction.
